clue.text: Vision of rook in flight

parts.note: the rook in chess is also called the castle
something in flight is up aloft, off the ground

explanation.surface: Someone imagines watching a rook, the black bird, flapping across the sky.
explanation.walkthrough: The bird is a decoy: the rook needed is the chess piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A castle in the air is an impractical dream or daydream, a fanciful imagined scheme.

clue.text: It gives no grounds for certain fees being changed

definitions.note: cryptic: it lets none of the coffee grounds through

indicators.note: things being changed are altered in form, so the letters are reordered

explanation.surface: A legal-sounding complaint that there is no justification for altering some charges.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grounds' looks like reasons or justification; here it is the dregs of brewed coffee.
explanation.definitionFit: A sieve for brewed coffee holds back the dregs, letting only liquid pass into the cup.

clue.text: Has performed star turn in holy writing

indicators.note: a piece performed is worked through and acted out, so its letters are reworked
a turn upsets the order, so the letters come out differently arranged

explanation.surface: A celebrity has played the headline act in a religious text.
explanation.walkthrough: 'star turn' reads as the headline act of a show, but splits into fodder and signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A shastra is a Hindu sacred treatise, a scripture setting out religious or legal teaching.

clue.text: It might bring boxer or flautist unexpected success

parts.words: It might bring boxer or flautist unexpected success
parts.note: surface reading: good fortune that falls on a fighter or a flute player
setter's reading: a boxer lands a punch by chance and a flautist breathes into the instrument, both a fortunate one

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase means a stroke of luck generally, but is literal for both a punch and a breath into a flute.
explanation.definitionFit: A chance stroke of fortune that brings about a favourable result nobody planned.

clue.text: Motorway up over ring of thick paint

indicators.note: in a down clue going up means this name is read from the bottom

parts.note: the M1, Britain's main north-south motorway, with 1 as I
over in the sense of finished, done with
a ring is round like the letter O

explanation.surface: A road turns upward over a band of heavy paint.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is Britain's London-to-Leeds motorway, often written with the digit read as I.
explanation.definitionFit: Impasto is paint laid on so heavily that brush or knife marks stand out in relief.

clue.text: Musical piece about animal wearing strange coat

indicators.note: one thing wearing another is clothed in it, so it sits inside
about means around, so the outer word goes round the other
strange suggests something odd and out of order, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A tune about a creature dressed up in an odd jacket.
explanation.definitionFit: A toccata is a keyboard composition for showing off rapid finger-work, such as Bach's famous one in D minor.

clue.text: Land on planet

definitions.meaning: second meaning: the world we live on

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests touching down somewhere in space; 'on' only joins the two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both the soil underfoot and the third world from the Sun.

clue.text: Silly of Intelligence Department when one's to be back in charge

indicators.note: to be back is to face the other way, so this short word is read from its end

parts.note: i/c is the standard abbreviation for in charge

explanation.surface: A spy agency acting foolishly when someone is reinstated as head.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiotic means stupid or foolish, behaving like a fool.

clue.text: Perhaps many like self to be hidden from outsiders?

definitions.note: describes the noun answer: something kept secret

indicators.note: perhaps hints the letters are one possible version of another arrangement

explanation.surface: Many people, like oneself, would prefer some things were kept private.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' looks like part of the phrase 'to be hidden', but it is counted among the letters being rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A family skeleton is a shameful household secret, kept from strangers as in skeleton in the cupboard.

clue.text: Headgear not worn by the Roundheads?

definitions.text: Headgear not worn by the Roundheads?

parts.words: Headgear not worn by the Roundheads?
parts.note: surface reading: the Parliamentarian soldiers of the English Civil War and their helmets
setter's reading: people whose heads are literally round would not wear something level on top

explanation.walkthrough: The Roundheads were Cromwell's side in the English Civil War; the joke takes their nickname literally and contrasts round with level.
explanation.definitionFit: A flat cap is the soft peaked cloth hat associated with British working men and countryside wear.

clue.text: Can take girl out in car

indicators.note: to take something is to hold it, so one piece is held by the other here
the girl is placed outside, wrapping round the other word

parts.note: a tin is a can of food

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether they may take a young woman out on a date in their car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' looks like the verb of asking permission but is the noun, a tin.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cortina was a popular Ford family saloon sold in Britain from the 1960s to the 1980s.

clue.text: Competitors in narrow lane

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the full field of contestants signed up for a race or event
second meaning: in northern England, a narrow passage between houses

explanation.surface: Racers squeezed together jostling in a tight alleyway.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is regional British: in the North an entry is an alley between terraced houses.
explanation.definitionFit: A race's entry is its collective list of competitors, and the dialect word names a small alley or passage.

clue.text: It is eaten from this Paget dish

definitions.note: a cryptic description standing for the foodstuff

indicators.note: to dish something is to ruin or wreck it, so these letters are broken up

explanation.surface: A diner is told to eat from the plate belonging to someone called Paget.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dish' reads as the plate but is a verb meaning spoil; the definition is the cryptic description at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Pasta in long thin strands is food, something that is consumed at meals.

clue.text: Logical as imitation stone?

indicators.note: an imitation is a mock copy, so the letters are refashioned into something else

explanation.surface: A question about whether reasoning can be as rigid as a fake rock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'imitation' does double service: it reworks the letters and, with stone, describes the material.
explanation.definitionFit: Scagliola is polished plasterwork with coloured chips, made to resemble marble and other decorative masonry.

clue.text: Folding seat is commonly shaky

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the fold-out rear seat of an old two-seater car
second meaning: colloquial British for unsound or weak, as in a bad heart

explanation.surface: A collapsible chair is often wobbly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'commonly' signals informal usage: a dicky heart or knee is a dodgy one.
explanation.definitionFit: A dicky seat was a hinged extra seat in a vintage car's boot, and the slang adjective means unreliable or feeble.

clue.text: Reckless person's turn of speed on bad road

indicators.note: a turn of something twists it round, so its letters are reordered
bad means in poor shape, so this word's letters are disordered

explanation.surface: A daredevil puts on a burst of speed on a poor road surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A desperado is a lawless, rash outlaw ready to take any risk.

clue.text: Frenchman with point to make good

parts.note: west, a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A Frenchman has a purpose to reform himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'point' is a compass point, one of N, S, E, W.
explanation.definitionFit: To renew something is to restore or repair it, bringing it back into a sound state.

clue.text: Less pleasant to set out in flurry of rain

indicators.note: in places one jumbled piece inside the other
out suggests disorder, so this short word is jumbled
a flurry is a confused swirl, so the letters are tossed about

explanation.surface: Setting off in a shower makes things more unpleasant.
explanation.definitionFit: Nastier is the comparative of nasty, meaning more disagreeable or unpleasant.

clue.text: One vet's staged lockout of cattle

indicators.note: something staged is arranged or set up for show, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: read as lock-out: the lock alone is used, its out acting as a second signal to rearrange

explanation.surface: A veterinary surgeon organises a lockout, shutting the farm animals away.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the 'lock' of lockout joins the fodder; its 'out' doubles as a second anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Livestock are farm animals collectively, of which cattle are the commonest example.

clue.text: Alter edited article pertaining to Roman church

indicators.note: edited text has been revised, so these letters are reordered

explanation.surface: An instruction to revise a piece of writing about the Catholic church.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lateran is the papal basilica of St John in Rome, the cathedral of the Pope as bishop of Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective refers to the Lateran palace and basilica in Rome, seat of famous church councils.

clue.text: Go away with king in glossy coat

indicators.note: with here means accompanied inside, so the monarch is placed within

parts.note: R for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A monarch is told to leave, dressed in a shiny robe.
explanation.definitionFit: Varnish is a transparent liquid finish that dries to a hard shiny layer on wood.

clue.text: Not in row following sketch

parts.note: a row of things is a line

explanation.surface: Someone left out of the queue behind a drawing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'following' just says the pieces come one after another; 'row' is a line, not a quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: An outline is a rough draft or summary drawing, giving only the main shape.

clue.text: Police officer who makes a dramatic call

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a rank of detective in the British police
second meaning: the visitor in J B Priestley's play An ... Calls

explanation.surface: A detective announces something startling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dramatic' points to the stage: in Priestley's play An Inspector Calls, the mysterious Inspector Goole visits a family.
explanation.definitionFit: An inspector is a senior police rank, and Priestley's title character is precisely one who calls in a drama.

clue.text: Poets thrown out of bar

indicators.note: thrown means tossed about, so the letters land in a new order

explanation.surface: Rowdy versifiers are ejected from a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bar' is not the pub but the legal verb; estop is a law term.
explanation.definitionFit: To estop is a legal term meaning to preclude or prevent a party from asserting something.

clue.text: Praise former setback

parts.note: ex- means former, as in ex-wife
set is a lot, a batch of items as at auction, and back turns it round

explanation.surface: Commending something that once was a setback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'setback' is printed as one word but splits into set and back.
explanation.definitionFit: To extol is to laud or glorify someone enthusiastically.

clue.text: He dispossesses oriental conqueror

parts.note: a victor is the one who wins

explanation.surface: An Eastern conquering ruler seizes property from his subjects.
explanation.definitionFit: An evictor is a person who throws tenants out of their home, removing their possession of it.

clue.text: He concentrated on poetry with one awful stigma

indicators.note: something awful is in a dreadful state, so its letters are messed up

explanation.surface: A poet focused on his verse despite carrying a terrible disgrace.
explanation.walkthrough: The Imagists, such as Ezra Pound, wrote spare, concentrated poetry built on precise images.
explanation.definitionFit: An Imagist belonged to the early twentieth-century movement favouring clear, compressed verse with sharp visual detail.

clue.text: Negligible amount needed to put hope into dancer, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints these letters are only one possible arrangement of another

explanation.surface: Only a tiny bit is required to give a dancer some optimism.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into' looks like a container signal, but it is part of the letters to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a contribution so small it makes no real difference to the whole.
